title: Resume UN-led negotiations on the Cyprus problem from where they stopped at Crans-Montana, on the basis of a bizonal, bicommunal federation
description: Sworn in on 28 February 2023, Christodoulides said that 'a solution to the Cyprus problem is my top priority'. In his first-year address (March 2024) he said the Greek Cypriot side was ready to negotiate 'on the basis of a bizonal, bicommunal federation, building on the negotiating acquis to date', and in September 2026 he asked the UN Secretary-General to convene an enlarged conference at which the resumption of negotiations 'from where they left off' (the 2017 Crans-Montana conference) would be announced.
reasoning: Concrete steps have been taken under UN auspices: informal enlarged meetings of the two leaders, the three guarantor powers and the UN in Geneva (March 2025) and New York (July 2025) agreed confidence-building measures, and Secretary-General Guterres, after visiting Cyprus in July 2026, said he would convene another '5+1' meeting after adequate preparation. But formal negotiations had not resumed by October 2026. According to the UN, sufficient common ground had not been found; the Turkish Cypriot leader Tufan Erhürman says he will start negotiations if Christodoulides accepts a rotating presidency in advance, which Christodoulides calls a precondition, and Turkey's President Erdoğan has called two states 'the most realistic solution'.
key_evidence: Geneva, March 2025: the leaders agreed six trust-building initiatives (four crossing points, demining, a youth technical committee, environment, solar energy in the buffer zone, cemeteries); Guterres spoke of a 'new atmosphere' (UN News)
New York, July 2025: four of the six initiatives achieved; the UN noted that common ground for resuming formal negotiations had not yet been found (UN News)
July 2026: Guterres' first official visit to Cyprus; he decided to convene another 5+1 meeting after preparations on confidence-building, methodology and substance (UN News)
13 November 2025: Turkish President Erdoğan, after meeting Erhürman, called the coexistence of two states the most realistic solution (Cyprus Mail)

20–22 October 2026: leaders' meeting under UN auspices; a trilateral meeting with UN envoy María Ángela Holguín scheduled for 9 November 2026; Erhürman says he would meet if Christodoulides 'explicitly and unconditionally accepts the rotating presidency'; Christodoulides says the Turkish side is setting preconditions (Cyprus Mail)

title: Obtain the appointment of a UN envoy to prepare the resumption of talks
description: To restart negotiations, Christodoulides asked UN Secretary-General António Guterres to appoint a special envoy on Cyprus.
reasoning: Guterres appointed the Colombian diplomat María Ángela Holguín Cuéllar as his personal envoy, who began work on the island in early 2024; Christodoulides said in March 2024 that her appointment was 'the result of our own persistent efforts and initiatives'. At the Geneva meeting of March 2025 all participants accepted the appointment of an envoy to prepare the next steps, and Holguín began a second term in May 2025. The appointment was obtained; whether it leads to negotiations is assessed under the separate promise on resuming talks.
key_evidence: March 2024: Christodoulides says Holguín's appointment and 'the beginning of a new effort to resume talks' resulted from his government's efforts (Cyprus Mail)
March 2025: Guterres cites 'the acceptance by all of the appointment of a Special Envoy on Cyprus to prepare the next steps' (UN News)
May 2025: Holguín's duties as envoy officially recommence for a second term (Cyprus Mail)

title: Secure a stronger EU role in the Cyprus settlement effort, including an EU envoy
description: From the start of his term Christodoulides made greater European Union involvement in efforts to restart negotiations a priority, arguing that 'the Cyprus problem is a European problem'.
reasoning: On 13 May 2025 the European Commission appointed Johannes Hahn as President von der Leyen's special envoy for the Cyprus problem, to work within the UN framework; Christodoulides called it 'the fruit of coordinated diplomatic efforts'. Hahn resigned in March 2026, and by September 2026 Commission Executive Vice-President Raffaele Fitto had been named EU special envoy for Cyprus. The Presidents of the European Council and of the Commission wrote jointly to the UN Secretary-General in 2025, and an EU–Turkey high-level meeting on creating conditions for talks was announced for October 2026 at Guterres' request. The Turkish Cypriot leadership of the time called Hahn's appointment 'a unilateral attempt' and said the EU could not be involved without its consent.
key_evidence: 13 May 2025: Hahn appointed Commission special envoy for the Cyprus problem; Turkish Cypriot leader Ersin Tatar objected (Cyprus Mail)
23 March 2026: Hahn resigns, citing other commitments (Cyprus Mail)
4 September 2026: Christodoulides cites the Costa–von der Leyen letter to the UN Secretary-General and the appointment of Raffaele Fitto as EU special envoy (Cyprus Mail)
16 October 2026: Christodoulides says an EU–Turkey meeting requested by Guterres will take place in October and that progress in EU–Turkey relations depends on resuming talks (Euronews)

title: A cabinet split 50/50 between women and men
description: On election night, 12 February 2023, Christodoulides pledged to keep his campaign promises, 'including making sure his Cabinet will be split 50/50 between men and women' (Cyprus Mail).
reasoning: The government announced on 27 February 2023 had 11 men and 6 women among ministers and deputy ministers, and women headed 3 of the 11 ministries; counting all 25 appointees (palace posts, undersecretaries, press staff, commissioners) there were 14 men and 11 women. The parity pledge was therefore not met for the cabinet itself; AKEL said he had 'raised the bar, but fell short' and former foreign minister Erato Kozakou-Marcoullis called the pledge 'a pre-election ploy'.
key_evidence: 27 February 2023: ministers and deputy ministers, 11 men and 6 women; 3 of 11 ministries headed by women (Cyprus Mail)
Of all 25 appointments announced, 14 were men and 11 women, 'though there were fewer females in key posts' (Reuters via VOA)

title: A government of technocrats who had not served in previous governments
description: During the campaign Christodoulides pledged a cabinet of technocrats who had not served before and to avoid appointing people who had served in past governments (Cyprus Mail; Reuters via VOA).
reasoning: His first cabinet included two former ministers: Finance Minister Makis Keravnos, who had held the same post under President Tassos Papadopoulos, and Interior Minister Constantinos Ioannou, health minister under Anastasiades. In the January 2024 reshuffle he appointed as defence minister Vasilis Palmas, a deputy minister under Anastasiades until 2022. Reuters described the shortfall as his first controversy.
key_evidence: 27 February 2023: Keravnos (finance minister under Papadopoulos) and Ioannou (health minister under Anastasiades) appointed (Cyprus Mail; VOA)
8 January 2024: Vasilis Palmas, former deputy minister in the Anastasiades government, appointed defence minister (Cyprus Mail)

title: Ensure Cyprus is not a destination country for irregular migrants
description: In his victory speech on 12 February 2023 Christodoulides said he would 'take the necessary steps to ensure Cyprus is not a destination country for illegal migrants' (Cyprus Mail).
reasoning: Parliament unanimously approved a Deputy Ministry of Migration and International Protection in February 2024; in April 2024 the government suspended the processing of asylum applications from Syrians; police reported 10,098 returns of irregular migrants in 2024. In September and October 2026 Christodoulides said arrivals had fallen by about 90–92% compared with 2022 and returns had risen by 180%. The verdict rests largely on government figures, and the methods are contested: Human Rights Watch reported in September 2024 that Cypriot authorities had pushed Syrian refugees back to Lebanon, which Cypriot officials deny.
key_evidence: 29 February 2024: House unanimously approves the bill creating the Deputy Ministry of Migration and International Protection (Cyprus Mail)
April 2024: processing of Syrian asylum applications suspended (Cyprus Mail; AP via Arab News)
10,098 irregular migrants returned in 2024, according to the police (Cyprus Mail, May 2025)
September 2026: Christodoulides cites a 92% fall in arrivals compared with 2022 and a 180% rise in returns (Cyprus Mail)
September 2024: Human Rights Watch report alleging pushbacks and collective expulsions (HRW)

title: Carry out the first comprehensive tax reform in more than two decades
description: Tax reform was 'one of the current administration's key policy planks' (Finance Minister Makis Keravnos). Christodoulides presented it as 'the first major tax reform in 23 years', prioritising support for Cypriot businesses (including cutting the special defence contribution on dividends from 17% to 5%) and for families and the middle class.
reasoning: On 22 December 2025 the House passed five of the six government tax bills, with amendments from the supporting parties DISY, DIKO, DIPA and EDEK; the reform took effect on 1 January 2026. It raised the income-tax-free threshold from €19,500 to €22,000 (the government had proposed €20,500), raised corporate tax from 12.5% to 15%, cut the defence contribution on dividends to 5%, abolished deemed dividend distribution for post-2026 profits and most stamp duties, and introduced an 8% tax on crypto-asset gains. AKEL called it 'socially unfair, lopsided and incomplete'.
key_evidence: 22 December 2025: five of six tax bills approved by majority (only the capital gains bill unanimously) (Cyprus Mail)
Tax-free threshold €22,000; corporate tax 15%; SDC on dividends 5%; in force 1 January 2026 (Cyprus Mail)

title: Join the Schengen area in 2026
description: On 11 May 2025 Christodoulides said: 'We will join the Schengen zone in 2026', promising that Cyprus would complete all technical requirements by the end of 2025.
reasoning: In September 2026 Christodoulides told European Council President António Costa that a European Commission evaluation had confirmed Cyprus' readiness and recommended completing the process as a priority. Accession, however, requires a unanimous decision of the Schengen states and a European Parliament vote, and none had been reported as of October 2026. The Green Line, not de jure an external border, is said to require strict controls (Cyprus Mail). With two months of 2026 left, the process is under way but the target year is not yet met.
key_evidence: 11 May 2025: 'We will join the Schengen zone in 2026' (Cyprus Mail)
4 September 2026: Christodoulides raises Cyprus' 'desire and readiness' for full accession with Costa, citing the Commission's evaluation (Cyprus Mail)

title: Open a maritime humanitarian corridor from Cyprus to Gaza (Amalthea initiative)
description: At the European Council of 26 October 2023 and the Paris Peace Forum in November 2023, Christodoulides proposed a sea corridor through which aid would be collected, inspected and stored in Cyprus and shipped to Gaza.
reasoning: On 8 March 2024 the European Commission, Cyprus, the UAE, the US, the UK and other states announced the opening of the corridor, stating that 'Cyprus' leadership in establishing the Amalthea Initiative … was integral'. The first ship, Open Arms, left Larnaca on 12 March 2024. According to the Cypriot foreign ministry, more than 37,000 tonnes of aid had been delivered by August 2026, now mostly via the Israeli port of Ashdod after the temporary US-built jetty was dismantled; the UN coordinator Sigrid Kaag said in 2024 that it could never replace land deliveries. The European Council backed the corridor again in October 2026.
key_evidence: 8 March 2024: joint statement endorsing the activation of the maritime corridor (European Commission, ECHO)
12 March 2024: first aid ship sails from Larnaca (Cyprus Mail)
August 2026: more than 37,000 tonnes delivered, according to the foreign ministry (Cyprus Mail, 17 October 2026)

title: Settle the cost-of-living allowance (CoLA) dispute, 'in its entirety by 2025'
description: The CoLA (ΑΤΑ), the automatic indexation of wages, was part of Christodoulides' campaign. The interim agreement his government brokered in May 2023 raised payment from 50% to 66.7% of the consumer price index and provided that 'the matter will be resolved in its entirety by 2025'.
reasoning: After failed talks and a three-hour general strike in September 2025, a permanent CoLA agreement was signed on 13 November 2025 in the presence of Christodoulides, within the 2025 deadline. It raises the rate to 80% from 1 January 2026, 90% from 1 July 2026 and 100% from 1 January 2027, paid in years of real GDP growth and capped at 4%, and extends CoLA to more than 55,000 additional beneficiaries according to the president. Employers called it 'a product of compromise'; the unions considered the result 'quite satisfactory'.
key_evidence: 12 May 2023: interim agreement, 66.7% of CPI, full resolution by 2025 (Cyprus Mail)
13 November 2025: permanent agreement signed; 80% → 90% → 100% by January 2027, 4% ceiling (Cyprus Mail)

title: Use the 2026 Cyprus presidency of the Council of the EU to bring the 2028–2034 EU budget to a negotiating framework with figures
description: The long-term EU budget (Multiannual Financial Framework, MFF) was one of the five priorities of the Cyprus presidency (January–June 2026), alongside defence and security, competitiveness, enlargement and citizens' rights; its stated objective was to present a mature negotiating framework.
reasoning: According to the presidency's own review, presented by Christodoulides at the European Council of 18–19 June 2026, it achieved 'its objective of presenting a mature negotiating framework, including financial figures', with partial general approaches on key financial instruments; European Council President Costa said the work left negotiators 'well positioned to move forward'. The assessment comes mainly from the presidency itself, and the final MFF deal, targeted for the end of 2026, was still under negotiation in October 2026.
key_evidence: 30 June 2026: the presidency concludes, reporting results on its five priorities (Cyprus Presidency)
19 June 2026: negotiating framework with figures presented; Costa and von der Leyen praise the presidency (Cyprus Presidency)
15–16 October 2026: MFF talks continue under the Irish presidency; Christodoulides says Cyprus had 'secured agreement on key aspects of the budget' (Cyprus Mail; Euronews)
